{{Orphan|date=March 2017}}
{{short description|Dimensionality reduction technique}}
In statistics, '''functional correlation''' is a [[dimensionality reduction]] technique used to quantify the [[correlation and dependence]] between two variables when the data is functional. Several approaches have been developed to quantify the relation between two functional variables.

==Overview==
A pair of real valued random functions  <math> \textstyle X(t)</math> and  <math> \textstyle Y(t)</math> with <math> t \in T</math>, a compact interval, can be viewed as realizations of [[square-integrable function|square-integrable]] [[stochastic process]] in a [[Hilbert space]]. Since both <math> X </math> and <math> Y </math>are infinite dimensional, some kind of [[dimensionality reduction|dimension reduction]] is required to explore their relationship. Notions of correlation for functional data include the following.<ref>Wang JL, Chiou JM, Müller HG. (2015). "Review of functional data analysis". ''Annual Reviews Statistics''. '''doi=10.1146'''</ref>

==Functional canonical correlation coefficient (FCCA)==

FCCA is a direct extension of multivariate [[canonical correlation]]. For a pair of random functions <math> X \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_X}) </math> and <math> Y \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y}) </math> the first canonical coefficient <math> \rho_1 </math> is defined as:
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">
\begin{align}\rho_1 &= \underset {u \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_X}) , v \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y})} {\sup} \operatorname{corr} (\langle u, X\rangle , \langle v, Y\rangle ) \\
& = \underset {u \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_X}) , v \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y})} {\sup}  \frac { \operatorname{cov} (\langle u, X\rangle , \langle v, Y\rangle )}{\sqrt{\operatorname{var}({\langle u, X\rangle})} \sqrt{\operatorname{var}({\langle v, Y\rangle})}} \\
& = \operatorname{corr} (\langle u_1, X\rangle , \langle v_1, Y\rangle )  
\end{align}</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
where <math>\langle \cdot,\cdot\rangle</math> denotes the [[Inner product space|inner product]] in [[Lp space]] (p=2) i.e. 
<math>\langle f_1,f_2\rangle = \int_{\mathcal{I}} f_1(t) f_2(t) \, dt, </math>  <math> \quad f_1, f_2 \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I}) </math>

The <math> k^{th}</math> canonical coefficient <math> \rho_k </math>, given <math>\rho_1, \rho_2, \ldots, \rho_{k-1} </math> is defined as:
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">\rho_k = \underset{\begin{matrix}u \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_X}), v \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y})\\ u \perp u_1,\ldots,u_{k-1}, v \perp v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}  \end{matrix}} {\sup} \frac {\operatorname{cov} (\langle u, X\rangle , \langle v, Y\rangle )}{\sqrt{\operatorname{var}(\langle u, X\rangle)} \sqrt{\operatorname{var}(\langle v, Y\rangle)} } = \operatorname{corr} (\langle u_k, X\rangle , \langle v_k, Y\rangle )</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

where <math> (U_k, V_k)=(\langle u_k, X\rangle , \langle v_k, Y\rangle )</math> is uncorrelated with all previous pairs <math>(U_j, V_j)=(\langle u_j, X\rangle , \langle v_j, Y\rangle )_{j=1,2,\ldots,k-1} </math>.

Thus FCCA implements projections in the directions of <math> U_k </math> and <math> V_k </math> for <math> X </math> and <math> Y </math> respectively, such that their linear combinations (inner products) <math> (U_k, V_k) </math> are maximally correlated. <math> X </math> and <math> Y </math> are uncorrelated if all their canonical correlations are zero, equivalently, if and only if <math> \rho_1 =0 </math>.

===Alternative formulation===
The [[cross-covariance]] operator for two random functions <math> X </math> and <math> Y </math> defined as <math> \Sigma_{XY} : \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_X}) \rightarrow \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y}) : \Sigma_{XY} v(t) = \int \operatorname{cov}( X(t), Y(t)) v(s) \, ds ;\quad v \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y}) </math> and analogously the auto covariance operators for <math> X,\Sigma_{XX} </math>, for <math> Y,\Sigma_{YY} </math> and using <math> \operatorname{cov} (\langle u, X\rangle , \langle v, Y\rangle ) =  \langle u, \Sigma_{XY}Y \rangle </math>, the <math> k^{th}</math> canonical coefficient <math> \rho_k </math> in (2) can be re-written as,
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">\rho_k = \underset{\begin{matrix}u \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_X}), v \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y})\\ u \perp u_1,\ldots,u_{k-1}, v \perp v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}  \end{matrix}}{\sup} \frac{\langle u, \Sigma_{XY}v \rangle }{\sqrt{\langle u, \Sigma_{XX}u \rangle}\sqrt{\langle v, \Sigma_{YY}v \rangle}}= \frac{\langle u_k, \Sigma_{XY}v_k \rangle }{\sqrt{\langle u_k, \Sigma_{XX}u_k \rangle}\sqrt{\langle v_k, \Sigma_{YY}v_k \rangle}}</math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}},
where <math> (U_k, V_k)=(\langle u_k, X\rangle , \langle v_k, Y\rangle )</math> is uncorrelated with all previous pairs <math>(U_j, V_j)=(\langle u_j, X\rangle , \langle v_j, Y\rangle )_{j=1,2,..,k-1} </math>

Maximizing (3) is equivalent to finding [[eigenvalues and eigenvectors]] of the operator <math> R= \Sigma^{-1/2}_{XX} \Sigma_{XY} \Sigma^{-1/2}_{YY} </math>.
===Challenges===
Since <math> \Sigma_{XX} </math> and <math> \Sigma_{YY} </math> are [[compact operator]]s, the square root of the auto-covariance operator of <math>  \mathcal{L^2}  </math> processes may not be invertible. So the existence of <math> R </math> and hence computing its [[eigenvalues and eigenvectors]] is an ill-posed problem. As a consequence of this inverse problem, [[overfitting]] may occur which may lead to an unstable correlation coefficient. Due to this inverse problem, <math> \rho_1</math> tends to be biased upwards and therefore close to 1 and hence is difficult to interpret. FCCA also requires densely recorded functional data so that the inner products in (2) can be accurately evaluated.

===Possible solutions===
Some possible solutions to this problem have been discussed.

* By restricting the maximization of (1) to discrete <math> l^2 </math> [[sequence space]]s  that are restricted to a [[reproducing kernel Hilbert space]] instead of entire <math>\mathcal{L}^2</math><ref> Eubank RL, Hsing T. (2008). "Canonical correlation for stochastic processes". ''Stochastic Processes and their applications'' '''118:1634-1661'''.</ref><ref> Yuan M, Cai TT. (2010). "A reproducing kernel Hilbert space approach to functional linear regression". '' The Annals of Statistics''. '''38:3412-3444.'''</ref>
* Using [[Cross-validation (statistics)|cross-validation]] to regularize the FCCA in practical implementation.<ref> He G, Müller HG, Wang JL. (2004). "Methods of canonical analysis for functional data".''Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference'' '''122(1):141–159'''</ref>

==Functional singular correlation analysis (FSCA)==

FSCA bypasses the inverse problem by simply replacing the objective function by covariance in place of correlation in (2). FSCA aims to quantify the dependency of <math> X,Y</math> by implementing the concept of functional [[singular-value decomposition]] for the [[cross-covariance]] operator. FSCA can be viewed as an extension of analyses using [[singular-value decomposition]] of vector data to functional data. For a pair of random functions <math> X \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_X}) </math> and <math> Y \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y}) </math> with smooth mean functions <math> \mu_X(t)=\mathbb{E}(X(t))</math> and <math> \mu_Y(t)=\mathbb{E}(Y(t))</math> and smooth covariance functions, FSCA aims at a "functional covariance" corresponding to the first singular value of the cross-covariance operator <math>\Sigma_{XY}</math>, 
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">\underset {u \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_X}) , v \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y})} {\sup} \operatorname{cov} (\langle u, X\rangle , \langle v, Y\rangle )=\underset {u \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_X}) , v \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y})} {\sup} \langle u, \Sigma_{XY}v \rangle </math> |{{EquationRef|4}}}}
which is attained at functions <math>u_1 \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_X}) , v_1 \in \mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{I_Y})</math>. A standardized version of this serves as a functional correlation and is defined as
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">\rho_1 = \frac{\langle u_1, \Sigma_{XY}v_1 \rangle}{\sqrt{\langle u_1, \Sigma_{XX}u_1 \rangle} \sqrt{\langle v_1, \Sigma_{YY}v_1 \rangle}}</math>|{{EquationRef|5}}}},
The singular representation of the cross-covariance can be employed to find a solution to the maximization problem (4).<ref>Yang W, Müller HG, Stadtmüller U. (2011). "Functional singular component analysis". '' Journal of Royal Statistical Society''. '''68(1):3–25'''</ref>
Analogously, we can extend this concept to find the next <math>k </math> ordered singular correlation coefficients <math> \rho_1, \rho_2,\ldots,\rho_k </math>.

==Correlation as angle between functions ==
In the multivariate case, the [[inner product]] of two vectors <math>a </math> and <math>b </math> is defined as, <math> \langle a,b \rangle = \|a\| \|b\| \cos\alpha</math> where <math> \alpha </math> is the angle between  <math>a </math> and <math>b </math>. This can be extended to the space of square integrable random functions. For this notion to be a meaningful measure of alignment of shapes, the integrals of the functions, which are the projections on the constant function 1, are subtracted. This part corresponds to a "static part" and the remainder can be thought of as a "dynamic part" for each random function. The cosine of the <math>L^2</math> angle between these "dynamic parts" then provides a correlation measure of functional shapes. Denoting <math> M_1=\langle X,1 \rangle</math> and <math> M_2=\langle Y,1 \rangle</math> the standardized curves may be defined as<ref>Dubin JA, Müller HG. (2005). "Dynamic correlation for multivariate longitudinal data". ''Journal of American Statistical Association''. '''100(471):872–881'''</ref><ref> Opgen-Rhein R, Strimmer K. (2006). "Inferring gene dependency networks from genomic longitudinal data : a function data approach". '' REVSTAT – Statistical Journal''. '''4:53–65'''</ref> <math display="block"> X^*(t)=\left(X(t)-M_1(t)\right) \Big / \left(\int (X(t)-M_1(t))^2 \, dt\right)^{1/2}</math>
<math display="block"> Y^*(t)=\left(Y(t)-M_2(t)\right) \Big / \left(\int (Y(t)-M_2(t))^2 \,dt\right)^{1/2}</math> and the correlation is defined as,
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">\rho = \mathbb{E} \langle X^*, Y^* \rangle </math>|{{EquationRef|6}}}}
